main.title: Meteos
main.summary: Meteos is a 2005 tile-matching video game developed by Q Entertainment and published by Bandai for the Nintendo DS.

cards.text: Meteos is a 2005 tile-matching video game developed by Q Entertainment and published by Bandai for the Nintendo DS. Nintendo released the game outside Japan. It was produced by Q Entertainment founder Tetsuya Mizuguchi and designed by Masahiro Sakurai. Meteos was inspired by the video game Missile Command (1980), the film The Matrix (1999) and the television series 24 (2001-2010).

The stylus moves coloured blocks called meteos as they fall from the top of the screen. Aligning three or more of the same colour launches them upwards, helping clear the growing stack. Play ends if the blocks fill the screen. Thirty-two alien characters and their respective planets give the different settings their identities.

Meteos received critical acclaim and reached number one in DS sales in the UK market during its first week, according to research company Chart-Track. It was compared to other puzzle games, such as Tetris (1985) and Lumines (2004). The game received awards and nominations from several publications, including the CESA Game Awards' Outstanding Performance Award. Versions were released for mobile phones and the Xbox Live Arcade in 2006 and 2008, respectively. A sequel, Meteos: Disney Magic, was released for the Nintendo DS in 2007.

main.title: God of War
main.subtitle: Kratos Enters Greek Myth as a Mechanical Force
main.summary: The original God of War builds Kratos around chained blades, mythological obstacles and a revenge story told in flashback.

cards.heading: A bargain with Ares
cards.text: Sony released God of War in North America on 22 March 2005 for PlayStation 2. Santa Monica Studio cast Kratos as a former Spartan whose pact with Ares leads to a revenge quest. The original story draws on Greek mythology; it is a different period of the character's life from the later Norse games.

cards.heading: Weapons that shape movement
cards.text: The Blades of Chaos attach to Kratos through chains, giving combat a distinctive reach and silhouette. Battles share the journey with climbing, rope swings, swimming and traps. A weapon animation or movement across a gap can therefore carry the same exaggerated physical force as the creatures being fought.

cards.heading: A journey through hostile architecture
cards.text: The campaign tells its backstory through flashbacks while driving Kratos towards Pandora's box and a confrontation with Ares. Mythological places become working obstacles: submerged ruins, sandstorms and a temple carried by a giant. Their scale is experienced through the actions needed to cross them, as well as through cinematic sequences.

cards.heading: The Challenge of the Gods and unlockable rewards
cards.text: When the game is completed, a challenge mode—ten trials called the Challenge of the Gods—is unlocked; this requires players to complete a series of specific tasks. The player may unlock bonus costumes for Kratos, behind-the-scenes videos, and concept art of the characters and environments, as rewards. Completion of each difficulty level unlocks additional rewards.

main.title: Kirby: Canvas Curse
main.summary: With Kirby transformed into a ball, the stylus draws the roads beneath him, changes his direction and keeps danger away while the ink supply recovers.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Kirby: Canvas Curse, released in Europe as Kirby: Power Paintbrush, is HAL Laboratory's 2005 Nintendo DS platform game. A witch turns Dream Land into a painting and Kirby into a ball. The player guides him through this painted world with the stylus, drawing paths and touching the action directly on the lower screen.

cards.heading: Draw the route, then let it run
cards.text: A rainbow line becomes a surface Kirby can roll along, carrying him in the direction it was drawn. An upward curve can reach a ledge; a wall placed in front of him can send him back the other way. Drawing also drains the ink gauge, which recovers while the brush is idle and refills faster when Kirby rests on solid ground. The route has to leave room for those pauses. A successful line gets him across a hazard without spending the ink needed for the next one.

cards.heading: A tap can change the encounter
cards.text: Touching Kirby gives him a short dash, while touching an enemy stuns it. The player can prepare a safe collision before Kirby arrives, or let a dash carry him into an opponent to take its Copy Ability. Tapping him then uses the copied power. The brush also reaches switches and breakable blocks, and rainbow lines can block incoming attacks. Movement and protection share the same hand: drawing a path may have to wait while an approaching obstacle needs immediate attention.

cards.heading: Give the brush another job
cards.text: The cleared stages return in Rainbow Run, where Time Trial rewards a quick finish and Line Trial restricts the amount of ink available. Medals earned in the adventure and these challenges can be exchanged for unlockables. The boss games give the stylus other tasks: Cart Run changes the height of a rail to carry Kirby past obstacles, while Block Attack uses drawn paddles to bounce him through blocks. The brush remains familiar, but the timing required of it keeps changing.

main.title: Wipeout Pure
main.subtitle: Anti-gravity racing arrives with the PSP
main.summary: Wipeout Pure is Studio Liverpool's PSP racing game, first released in North America on 24 March 2005. The FX300 league brings anti-gravity craft to a portable screen, combining high speed with airbrakes, weapons and sharply defined circuits. Set a century after Wipeout 2097, it returns to a cleaner visual direction after Wipeout Fusion. Each team offers a craft with its own balance of handling, acceleration, speed and shields. Choosing one is the beginning of learning how to carry momentum through a course without allowing the next corner to turn it into a collision.

cards.heading: Anti-gravity racing arrives with the PSP
cards.text: Wipeout Pure is Studio Liverpool's PSP racing game, first released in North America on 24 March 2005. The FX300 league brings anti-gravity craft to a portable screen, combining high speed with airbrakes, weapons and sharply defined circuits. Set a century after Wipeout 2097, it returns to a cleaner visual direction after Wipeout Fusion. Each team offers a craft with its own balance of handling, acceleration, speed and shields. Choosing one is the beginning of learning how to carry momentum through a course without allowing the next corner to turn it into a collision.

cards.heading: A pickup can keep the craft alive
cards.text: Weapon pickups can be used against opponents or absorbed to replenish the shield, connecting attack and survival to the same resource. A player near the front may prefer to preserve a damaged craft rather than risk it for another shot. Airbrakes and careful positioning remain essential as the circuits become faster and more demanding. Knowing the route helps identify where to commit to speed and where a slight correction is worth more. The race becomes a continuing balance between the line ahead, the condition of the craft and the rivals sharing the track.

cards.heading: A portable demonstration with room to grow
cards.text: Development began in 2003 and continued through the PSP's North American launch, with new interface and production tools helping the team complete the game in time. Reviews praised its appearance, course design and overall presentation, while noting occasional performance fluctuations. Japanese and European editions followed in April and September 2005. Downloadable additions later enlarged the collection of tracks and craft. Pure became a strong demonstration of the handheld's possibilities by carrying a recognisable console series into a portable format while preserving the speed, visual discipline and musical character that defined it.

main.title: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory
main.summary: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is a 2005 action-adventure stealth game co-developed by Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Milan, and published by Ubisoft.

cards.text: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is a 2005 action-adventure stealth game co-developed by Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Milan, and published by Ubisoft. The game was released for GameCube, PlayStation 2, Windows and Xbox in March 2005. Handheld versions for the Nintendo DS, mobile, and N-Gage were also released.

Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory is the sequel to Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow and the third game in the Splinter Cell series endorsed by novelist Tom Clancy. As with previous entries in the franchise, Chaos Theory follows the activities of Sam Fisher, an agent working for a covert-ops branch within the NSA called "Third Echelon". The game has a significantly darker tone than its predecessors, featuring more combat and the option for Fisher to kill people he interrogates instead of merely knocking them out. As a result, it was the first Splinter Cell game to receive an M-rating by the ESRB, an assessment which has since been applied to all subsequent releases in the series. Actor Michael Ironside reprised his role as Fisher. Don Jordan returned from the original game to voice Third Echelon director Irving Lambert, and Claudia Besso returned as the hacker and analyst Anna Grímsdóttir, having both been replaced by Dennis Haysbert and Adriana Anderson, respectively, in Pandora Tomorrow.

Chaos Theory's Xbox and PC versions of the game received critical acclaim; the GameCube and PlayStation 2 iterations were also released to generally positive reviews. Chaos Theory was a commercial success, selling 2.5 million units across all platforms within a month of its release. Official Xbox Magazine named it the Xbox "Game of the Year" (2005) for its strong gameplay and lifelike graphics, and it received the highest-ever review score for the magazine at the time. It is considered one of the greatest video games ever made. Another port titled Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell 3D was released for the Nintendo 3DS in March 2011. A remastered high definition version was released on PlayStation 3 in September 2011, and an Xbox version was made available for Xbox One via backward compatibility in June 2019. A sequel, titled Double Agent, released in 2006.

main.title: Archer Maclean's Mercury
main.subtitle: Tilt the world beneath a drop of liquid metal
main.summary: Archer Maclean's Mercury is Awesome Studios' PSP puzzle-platform game, first released in North America on 6 April 2005. The player tilts a stage to guide a drop of mercury towards its destination. Unlike a solid ball, the material can stretch and divide, making its physical behaviour part of the problem. A narrow passage or exposed edge has to be approached with an awareness of what the liquid will do next. The game asks for careful control of the surroundings rather than direct movement of a character, giving gravity the role of the player's intermediary.

cards.heading: Tilt the world beneath a drop of liquid metal
cards.text: Archer Maclean's Mercury is Awesome Studios' PSP puzzle-platform game, first released in North America on 6 April 2005. The player tilts a stage to guide a drop of mercury towards its destination. Unlike a solid ball, the material can stretch and divide, making its physical behaviour part of the problem. A narrow passage or exposed edge has to be approached with an awareness of what the liquid will do next. The game asks for careful control of the surroundings rather than direct movement of a character, giving gravity the role of the player's intermediary.

cards.heading: A small movement can send the drop too far
cards.text: Tilting changes the direction and momentum of the mercury, so reaching a safe position often means beginning to slow it before the destination is reached. Different stages emphasise different tasks and obstacles, asking the player to adapt the same physical control to another arrangement. The unusual material gives an ordinary slope more consequences than it would have for a rigid object. The player has to watch the shape of the drop as well as its location, treating the stage as something that can pull the liquid apart or carry it towards the goal.

cards.heading: A physics experiment becomes a portable puzzle series
cards.text: Archer Maclean developed the idea from a small activity in Jimmy White's Cueball World, adding liquid-metal behaviour to create a distinct puzzle. An intended tilt-sensor accessory for PSP did not reach release because of technical limitations, leaving the finished game controlled through the handheld's ordinary inputs. Reviews welcomed the concept and level design while noting the difficulty. Its success led to Mercury Meltdown and Mercury Hg. The original's clarity comes from a recognisable physical action: alter the slope, observe the material and make the next adjustment before momentum turns a useful movement into a loss.

main.title: Jade Empire
main.subtitle: Martial arts and choices in a BioWare fantasy
main.summary: Jade Empire arrived on Xbox in North America on April 12, 2005 and moved BioWare away from the licensed worlds that had helped establish its reputation.

cards.heading: An original world for BioWare
cards.text: Jade Empire is BioWare's Xbox role-playing adventure set in an original world drawing on Chinese folklore, culture and martial-arts cinema. Combat uses movement, dodges and changes of fighting style in real time. Companions, conversations and moral choices continue the studio's earlier approach to character-driven adventures. The North American release arrived on April 12, 2005, after BioWare's work in the licensed settings of Dungeons & Dragons and Star Wars.

cards.heading: A fantasy shaped by folklore and martial arts
cards.text: Architecture, costume, creatures, philosophy and wuxia cinema supply influences for Jade Empire's fantasy setting. Creating its own world allowed BioWare to combine those sources around the journey and its conflicts. The project followed games built within established licences, giving the studio an opportunity to develop a setting whose rules and history it could shape itself.

cards.heading: Changing styles during a fight
cards.text: Martial styles, weapons, magic and support techniques offer different approaches to a fight. The player can switch between them during combat, responding to an opponent through timing and positioning as well as character growth. Motion capture and animation help distinguish their rhythms. Reading an enemy and selecting a useful style puts the RPG's abilities into a continuous sequence of movements.

cards.heading: Open Palm and Closed Fist
cards.text: The Way of the Open Palm and the Way of the Closed Fist organise many decisions. Their opposing attitudes concern helping others preserve their independence or imposing strength, with companions responding according to their own histories. Conversations and alliances give these choices a personal setting. The player encounters their consequences through relationships alongside the journey's fights.

main.title: Unreal Championship 2: The Liandri Conflict
main.subtitle: The arena closes to striking distance
main.summary: Unreal Championship 2: The Liandri Conflict is Epic Games' Xbox arena shooter, first released in North America on 18 April 2005. It takes the Unreal series' fast competitive battles and gives melee weapons a central place beside firearms. Switching to a blade or staff changes the view to third person, making the character's movement easier to read at close range. The result is a contest between distances as well as weapons. An opponent across the room and one about to strike demand different responses from the same player.

cards.heading: The arena closes to striking distance
cards.text: Unreal Championship 2: The Liandri Conflict is Epic Games' Xbox arena shooter, first released in North America on 18 April 2005. It takes the Unreal series' fast competitive battles and gives melee weapons a central place beside firearms. Switching to a blade or staff changes the view to third person, making the character's movement easier to read at close range. The result is a contest between distances as well as weapons. An opponent across the room and one about to strike demand different responses from the same player.

cards.heading: Choose a fighter, then use their movement
cards.text: Characters belong to light, medium or heavy classes, with different balances of health, speed and striking power. A quick fighter can approach an encounter differently from a slower, stronger one, making movement part of the initial choice. Adrenaline abilities offer further ways to alter a confrontation. Firearms can be used from first- or third-person views, while close combat rewards attention to the opponent's position. The player learns when to keep firing, when to close the gap and when to escape before an enemy's advantage becomes decisive.

cards.heading: A console branch of Unreal
cards.text: The game was designed around Xbox Live competition, with additional characters and content released through the service. Its modes include familiar arena objectives alongside variations such as Overdose and Nali Slaughter. Kevin Riepl composed the score, while Midway published the release. The combination of acrobatic movement, character differences and melee combat gave this sequel a particular identity within Unreal. Rather than simply reproducing the PC tournament format, it used the console setting to rearrange the relationship between the fighter on screen, the camera and the next attack.

main.title: Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance
main.subtitle: A mercenary takes command
main.summary: Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance brings the tactical role-playing series to GameCube and introduces Ike, a young mercenary on the continent of Tellius. After Daein invades Crimea, his company becomes involved in Princess Elincia’s attempt to reclaim her kingdom. The journey crosses a world divided between the human beorc and the transforming laguz. Its political conflict gives the battles a context beyond advancing an army across a map, while Ike’s position outside the nobility supplies a different starting point for the adventure.

cards.heading: A mercenary takes command
cards.text: Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance brings the tactical role-playing series to GameCube and introduces Ike, a young mercenary on the continent of Tellius. After Daein invades Crimea, his company becomes involved in Princess Elincia’s attempt to reclaim her kingdom. The journey crosses a world divided between the human beorc and the transforming laguz. Its political conflict gives the battles a context beyond advancing an army across a map, while Ike’s position outside the nobility supplies a different starting point for the adventure.

cards.heading: The cost of a position
cards.text: Battles unfold on a grid, with each unit’s movement, weapon and role shaping its useful position. Sending a fighter forward can open a route and expose that fighter to several enemies at once. Experience makes survivors stronger, so protecting a familiar unit also protects the time invested in it. Permanent losses give mistakes a lasting consequence. The tactical question is therefore rarely just whether an enemy can be defeated this turn; it is whether the resulting arrangement leaves the company able to survive the next one.

cards.heading: Tellius in three dimensions
cards.text: Path of Radiance was the series’ first fully three-dimensional entry, returning Fire Emblem to a home console after its Game Boy Advance games. The larger presentation serves a campaign still built around individual units and their place in a growing company. Tellius also gives the series a setting it can revisit: Radiant Dawn later continues its history on Wii. Here, the contrast between peoples and social positions remains central to the journey, linking the movement of armies with the people affected by the war.

main.title: Nintendogs
main.subtitle: Touching the Screen Changed What a Handheld Could Mean
main.summary: Caring for virtual puppies introduced the Nintendo DS touch screen and microphone through familiar gestures.

cards.heading: Caring for a puppy on Nintendo DS
cards.text: Nintendogs is built around caring for virtual puppies on Nintendo DS. Players stroke a dog with the stylus, call it by name through the microphone and return to feeding, walks and training as time passes. These familiar activities make the handheld's unusual controls easy to understand. The game also provides a connection with National Dog Day, observed on August 26 and founded in 2004 to celebrate companion and working dogs and encourage adoption.

cards.heading: A stroke of the stylus
cards.text: Petting a puppy introduces the touch screen through a familiar movement. The stylus follows its back, face or fur, and the dog responds to the contact. A player can understand the gesture before learning conventional button combinations. The interaction gives the animal a presence on the screen and turns a hardware feature into part of caring for it.

cards.heading: Teaching a spoken command
cards.text: The microphone lets players call their dog by name and teach spoken commands. Repetition, waiting and watching for a response become part of the training. Recognition can be imperfect, but a puppy's variable response fits the game's domestic setting. Holding the DS close enough to speak to it gives these sessions a different feel from a game controlled entirely by buttons.

cards.heading: Returning for the next walk
cards.text: Feeding, walks and training encourage regular short visits. The system clock spreads these activities across real time, giving the player's return a purpose. Progress comes through this routine and the small changes noticed in a familiar animal. Its understandable goals helped show how Nintendo DS could reach people with little interest in conventional campaigns or score-based competition.
